Twenty-seven comments

Another reel made popular by M. Coleman - it’s often paired with Ballinsloe Fair. It’s a chicken & the egg situation, no ones sure if he paired them together & made the set famous - or if it was something he learned. Many times anything recorded by Coleman is attributed to his inovation - however a lot of the things he recorded were already traditional in Co. Sligo , but brand new to the rest of ITM (at the time). Some of those settings became standards.

This reel is a lot easier than it looks due to the 2nd & 4th parts being almost identical, except for the rolls/triplets on the d.

↳ Posted by Dr. Tøm on December 21st, 2011.

There’s worse…. :-P Way back when every ‘gan ainm’ in the book piled up as a recording someone was going around adding ‘gan ainm’ as a alternate title for many things, with the recording list exploding because of that addition. Since then Jeremy has sorted that out, but we still have misdirected connections and folks adding alternate titles as a kind of digital graffiti. Sometimes it helps to drop a quick note to the original submitter and sometimes they will come back and clean up the alternate titles list. Where there is a shared name or a confusion of names it is probably best to just mention it in the comments here and not add it to the list of alternate titles…

This might need to be opened up as a ‘discussion’?

Queen of the May?

The clown who linked Lord MacDonald’s to QotM is… Matt Molloy.
Or at least whoever listed the titles on Music at Matt Molloy’s. Clearly the tune on that recording is Lord MacDonald’s, but it follows Dr.Gilbert’s and so whoever titled it probably got confused with the Coleman set. All this is clear when you cross-check tune entries on TheSession, though I’m sure I wouldn’t have figured it out otherwise. I didn’t enter it originally as an alternate title but I see how it happened.
The careful stewards at TheSession have reversed the error introduced by “Folk process” however. I see it’s been removed as an alternate title, and in Recordings it shows the right titles. Good work.

Lord McDonald’s, X:12

This setting of the reel is from the power manuscript from Kilmore in County Wexford. It’s from the oldest part of the manuscript, which probably dates from the mid 19th century. There are some dated pieces from the ‘middle’ section (1872, 1880) so the earliest selection of material is prior to those dates and features very florid handwriting for tune titles and lovely copperplate writing. The middle section is clearly notated and written by a different person to the first section , and the ‘last section, which has some pieces dated 1920, is also clearly written by a third person. (different notation style and handwriting etc). Additionally there are some blank or partially blank staved pages where a young child has ’drawn in‘ random notes on stave lines , including a nonsense sequence of notes titled in the child’s writing ’Waltz 1919’.

Re: Lord McDonald’s

These days it’s quite widely accepted that the composer was Alexander MacDonald (1744–1795), an aristocratic fiddler, and composer from Sleat, Isle of Skye.

It’s become a classic in Scotland, Ireland and North America, so let’s give the guy some credit!
